newsitem.title: ITALY: IMF sees Italy '97 deficit/GDP at four pct - paper.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees Italy '97 deficit/GDP at four pct - paper.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts Italy's budget deficit will be four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997, financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said on Tuesday.

This meant Italy needed extra budget deficit cutting measures worth 20 trillion lire this year if it wanted to reach the three percent deficit to GDP ratio required to join a European single currency in 1999, the newspaper reported.
The paper said the forecasts were contained in a draft of the IMF's World Economic Outlook due to be presented to finance ministers in Washington in the next few weeks.

Il Sole said the IMF report also saw France and Germany outside the Maastricht treaty requirements concerning deficit to GDP ratios, with Germany's deficit to stand at 3.3 percent of GDP by the year end and France at 3.4 percent.
In all three countries "urgent corrective" budgetary measures, of a permanent rather than stop-gap character, were necessary, the newspaper said.

But France and Germany had better growth outlooks for this year then Italy. German growth was forecast at two percent and French growth at 2.25 percent, while the outlook for Italy had been cut to one percent from two estimated last September.
Average Italian inflation was forecast at 2.7 percent for 1997 while French inflation was predicted at 1.5 percent and in Germany at 1.9 percent.
The Italian government is expected to unveil a mini-budget for 1997 later this week which is expected to be for 15 to 16 trillion of budget deficit cutting measures.

Il Sole said that on the basis of the IMF calculations a 16 trillion lire mini-budget would be insufficient. "In order to be certain to enter the three percent territory... the mini budget needs to be equal to one percent of the estimates for GDP, so equivalent to 20 trillion lire," it said.
Even if the figure was adequate, in order for the mini budget to have the desired effect it needed to contain measures aimed at permanent long-term cuts in spending.
It said the IMF's idea was that the mini budget represented the last possibility for Italy successfully to complete a cycle of hard budgets and important agreements with unions.
"Today the structural component is the most important to give credibility to the proposals for rigour in the medium term in Italy," the paper quoted a monetary source as saying.
"I hope that in the brief space of time which remains available the energy which the country has invested up to now will not be wasted," the source said.
